topics.title: Functions, composites and inverses
points: A function has one \(y\)-value for each \(x\). State the domain (allowed \(x\)) and range (resulting \(y\)).
The composite \(f(g(x))\) exists only if \(\operatorname{ran}(g) \subseteq \operatorname{dom}(f)\).

An inverse \(f^{-1}\) exists only for a one-to-one function: swap \(x\) and \(y\) and solve. Its graph is the reflection of \(f\) in \(y = x\); \(\operatorname{dom}(f^{-1}) = \operatorname{ran}(f)\) and \(\operatorname{ran}(f^{-1}) = \operatorname{dom}(f)\).
Transformations: \(y = a f\big(b(x - h)\big) + k\). Describe them as dilations, reflections, then translations, or as a mapping \((x, y) \to (x', y')\).
Sum or product of functions: the domain is \(\operatorname{dom}(f) \cap \operatorname{dom}(g)\).
topics.explain: Explain why \(y = x^2\) needs a restricted domain to have an inverse function.

qs.q: Find the inverse of \(f(x) = 2x + 3\).
The graph of \(f^{-1}\) is the reflection of \(f\) in…
State the maximal domain of \(f(x) = \log_e(x - 2)\).
The maximal domain of \(f(x) = \log_e(2x - 4)\) is…
Find the inverse of \(f: [1, \infty) \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = (x - 1)^2 + 3\), with its domain.
s: The range of \(f\) is \([3, \infty)\); this becomes the domain of \(f^{-1}\).
\(y - 1 = \pm\sqrt{x - 3}\). The range of \(f^{-1}\) must be \([1, \infty)\), so take the positive root.

qs.q: \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and \(g(x) = x - 5\), each on its maximal domain. Does \(f \circ g\) exist? If not, how could \(g\) be restricted?
s: \(\operatorname{ran} g = \mathbb{R}\) but \(\operatorname{dom} f = [0, \infty)\), so it does not exist.
Restricting \(g\) to \([5, \infty)\) makes its range \([0, \infty)\), and then \(f(g(x)) = \sqrt{x - 5}\).

qs.q: The image of \(y = e^x\) under a dilation by factor 2 from the \(y\)-axis is…
Which function is odd, so that f(−x) = −f(x)?

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the Units 1 and 2 lessons on functions, polynomials, exponentials, logarithms and circular functions.

The big idea: Units 3 and 4 treat functions as objects that can be combined, reversed and transformed. Questions are more precise than in Units 1 and 2: every function comes with a domain, and many marks depend on stating domains and ranges exactly. This lesson is the language that the calculus and probability lessons rely on.

A function is written with its domain and rule: \(f: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = \sqrt{x}\). If no domain is given, use the maximal (implied) domain: all \(x\) for which the rule is defined. Watch for three restrictions: no division by zero, no even root of a negative, no logarithm of a non-positive number.
A function is one-to-one if each \(y\)-value comes from only one \(x\)-value (horizontal line test). Otherwise it is many-to-one.

\(f \circ g\) means apply \(g\) first, then \(f\): \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\). It is defined only if every output of \(g\) is an allowed input of \(f\), that is \(\operatorname{ran} g \subseteq \operatorname{dom} f\). When defined, its domain is the domain of \(g\).

Example: \(f(x) = \log_e x\) (domain \(x > 0\)) and \(g(x) = x - 2\) (range \(\mathbb{R}\)). \(f \circ g\) is not defined, because \(g\) outputs negative numbers. Restrict \(g\) to \(x > 2\): then its range is \((0, \infty)\) and \(f(g(x)) = \log_e(x - 2)\) with domain \((2, \infty)\).

The inverse undoes the function. Its graph is the reflection in \(y = x\), so \(\operatorname{dom} f^{-1} = \operatorname{ran} f\) and \(\operatorname{ran} f^{-1} = \operatorname{dom} f\). A many-to-one function needs its domain restricted before it has an inverse function.

Example: \(f: [1, \infty) \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = (x - 1)^2 + 2\). Swap: \(x = (y - 1)^2 + 2\), so \(y = 1 \pm \sqrt{x - 2}\). The range of \(f^{-1}\) must be \([1, \infty)\), so take the positive root: \(f^{-1}(x) = 1 + \sqrt{x - 2}\), with domain \([2, \infty)\).
A function and its inverse meet on the line \(y = x\) when the function is increasing, so solving \(f(x) = x\) is usually easiest.

To find the image of a graph, replace \(x\) and \(y\) in the rule. A dilation by factor 2 from the \(y\)-axis replaces \(x\) with \(\tfrac{x}{2}\). A translation 3 units right replaces \(x\) with \(x - 3\). To find the transformations that map one graph to another, write both in a matching form and compare.

Example: map \(y = \sqrt{x}\) to \(y = 2\sqrt{3 - x} + 1\). Write it as \(y = 2\sqrt{-(x - 3)} + 1\): dilation by factor 2 from the \(x\)-axis, reflection in the \(y\)-axis, then translation 3 units right and 1 unit up. Order matters: dilations and reflections first, then translations, when reading from this form.

Sum, difference and product functions are defined only where both functions are defined. Graphs can be built by adding ordinates. A piecewise (hybrid) function has different rules on different parts of its domain; check each endpoint for an open or closed circle and for continuity.

notes.h: Worked example: inverse of an exponential
p: Find the inverse of \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R},\ f(x) = 2e^{x - 1} + 3\). First, the range of \(f\): \(e^{x - 1} > 0\), so \(f(x) > 3\), giving range \((3, \infty)\).

Swap and solve: \(x = 2e^{y - 1} + 3 \Rightarrow e^{y - 1} = \dfrac{x - 3}{2} \Rightarrow y = 1 + \log_e\!\left(\dfrac{x - 3}{2}\right)\). So \(f^{-1}: (3, \infty) \to \mathbb{R},\ f^{-1}(x) = 1 + \log_e\!\left(\dfrac{x - 3}{2}\right)\). The asymptote \(y = 3\) of \(f\) becomes the asymptote \(x = 3\) of \(f^{-1}\).
check: Find the inverse of \(f(x) = e^x + 2\) and its domain.

fig.cap: f(x) = 2e^(x − 1) + 3 and its inverse f⁻¹(x) = 1 + logₑ((x − 3)/2): reflections in y = x, with asymptotes y = 3 and x = 3.

p: A sequence of transformations can be written as a mapping of points. Dilating by factor 3 from the \(x\)-axis and then translating 1 unit right sends \((x, y)\) to \((x + 1, 3y)\). Under this mapping \(y = x^2\) becomes \(y = 3(x - 1)^2\): the point \((2, 4)\) moves to \((3, 12)\), and \(3(3 - 1)^2 = 12\) confirms it.

To find the rule of an image from a mapping \((x, y) \to (x', y')\), solve for \(x\) and \(y\) in terms of \(x'\) and \(y'\) and substitute into the original rule. Here \(x = x' - 1\) and \(y = \dfrac{y'}{3}\), so \(\dfrac{y'}{3} = (x' - 1)^2\).
check: Find the image of \((1, 1)\) under the mapping \((x, y) \to (x - 2, 4y)\).

p: Some questions ask whether a function satisfies a property for all values. Substitute into both sides and compare. \(f(x) = \log_e x\): \(f(xy) = \log_e(xy) = \log_e x + \log_e y = f(x) + f(y)\), so \(f(xy) = f(x) + f(y)\) holds. \(f(x) = e^x\): \(f(x + y) = e^{x + y} = e^x e^y = f(x)f(y)\). \(f(x) = x^2\): \(f(-x) = f(x)\), so the function is even.
To show a property is false, one counterexample is enough. For \(f(x) = x + 1\), \(f(1 \times 1) = 2\) but \(f(1) + f(1) = 4\), so \(f(xy) = f(x) + f(y)\) does not hold.

Writing \(f^{-1}(x)\) as \(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\). Leaving out the domain of an inverse. Choosing the wrong branch of the square root. Testing \(\operatorname{dom} g \subseteq \operatorname{dom} f\) in place of the range condition for a composite.

topics.title: Solving equations
points: Exponential and log equations: use the log laws; check every solution is in the domain.
Circular equations: find the base angle, then use symmetry (ASTC) and add periods to get all solutions in the domain.
General solution: \(\sin x = a \Rightarrow x = \sin^{-1}(a) + 2n\pi\) or \(x = \pi - \sin^{-1}(a) + 2n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
Simultaneous linear equations can have a unique solution, infinitely many, or none.
Use CAS where allowed, but write the set-up.
topics.explain: Explain why \(2\sin x = 1\) has two solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\).

qs.q: Solve \(2\sin(x) = 1\) for \(x \in [0, 2\pi]\).
Solve \(\log_e x + \log_e(x - 3) = \log_e 4\).
s: \(x = -1\) is rejected because \(\log_e(-1)\) is undefined. So \(x = 4\).

qs.q: Find the general solution of \(2\sin x = 1\).
s: \(\sin x = \tfrac{1}{2}\); the solutions in \([0, 2\pi]\) are \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\) and \(\tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).
Sine repeats every \(2\pi\), so add \(2n\pi\) to each.

qs.q: The solutions of \(e^{2x} - 5e^x + 6 = 0\) are…
Solve \(\cos 2x = 0\) for \(0 \le x \le \pi\).
For which values of \(m\) do \(mx + 3y = 6\) and \(2x + (m - 1)y = 4\) have no solution, and for which infinitely many?
s: The lines are parallel when \(\dfrac{m}{2} = \dfrac{3}{m - 1}\), so \(m(m - 1) = 6\), giving \(m = 3\) or \(m = -2\).
\(m = 3\): the equations are \(3x + 3y = 6\) and \(2x + 2y = 4\), the same line, so infinitely many solutions.
\(m = -2\): \(-2x + 3y = 6\) and \(2x - 3y = 4\) are parallel and different, so no solution.
Every other value of m gives a unique solution.

qs.q: The exact solution of \(5e^x = 20\) is…
Find the general solution of \(\tan x = \sqrt{3}\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the functions lesson, log laws and exact values of circular functions.

The big idea: most questions in Methods end in an equation. This lesson collects the methods for each family, shows how to handle parameters and restricted domains, and explains when to use technology. Accuracy here is what turns understanding into marks.

Bring everything to one side and factorise. For cubics and quartics, find a root with the factor theorem, divide, and continue. A literal equation contains parameters; solve it in terms of them and state any restrictions.
Hidden quadratics appear often: \(x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0\) with \(u = x^2\) gives \(u = 1, 4\), so \(x = \pm 1, \pm 2\).
Example: \(e^{2x} - 3e^x - 4 = 0\). Let \(u = e^x\): \((u - 4)(u + 1) = 0\). \(e^x = -1\) has no solution because \(e^x > 0\), so \(x = \log_e 4\).
Example: \(2\log_e x - \log_e(x + 6) = 0\). \(\log_e\dfrac{x^2}{x + 6} = 0 \Rightarrow x^2 = x + 6 \Rightarrow x = 3\) or \(x = -2\). Reject \(-2\), since \(\log_e(-2)\) is undefined.

Over a restricted domain, find the reference angle, choose quadrants by sign, and list every solution in the domain, adjusting the domain first for \(nx\). A general solution gives all solutions with \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\): for \(\sin x = a\), \(x = 2n\pi + \sin^{-1}a\) or \(x = (2n + 1)\pi - \sin^{-1}a\); for \(\cos x = a\), \(x = 2n\pi \pm \cos^{-1}a\); for \(\tan x = a\), \(x = n\pi + \tan^{-1}a\).
Example: \(\sin 2x = \cos 2x\). Divide by \(\cos 2x\) (which is not zero at a solution): \(\tan 2x = 1\), so \(2x = n\pi + \tfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(x = \tfrac{n\pi}{2} + \tfrac{\pi}{8}\).

Two lines \(ax + by = e\) and \(cx + dy = f\) meet once if their gradients differ. If the gradients are equal there is no solution when the lines are parallel and distinct, and infinitely many when they are the same line.

Example: \(kx + 2y = 4\) and \(8x + ky = 8\). Equal gradients: \(-\tfrac{k}{2} = -\tfrac{8}{k}\), so \(k = \pm 4\). For \(k = 4\) the lines are \(4x + 2y = 4\) and \(8x + 4y = 8\), which are identical: infinitely many solutions. For \(k = -4\) they are \(-4x + 2y = 4\) and \(8x - 4y = 8\), which are parallel and distinct: no solution. A unique solution exists for all other \(k\).

When an equation cannot be solved exactly, use a numerical method. Newton’s method improves an estimate using the tangent: \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\). It can fail if a starting value is near a stationary point, where the tangent is nearly horizontal.

notes.h: Worked example: a shifted circular equation
p: Solve \(2\cos\left(2x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1\) for \(0 \le x \le \pi\). Let \(\theta = 2x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}\). Since \(0 \le x \le \pi\), \(-\tfrac{\pi}{3} \le \theta \le \tfrac{5\pi}{3}\).

\(\cos\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}\) on that interval gives \(\theta = -\tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \tfrac{5\pi}{3}\). Then \(2x = \theta + \tfrac{\pi}{3}\), so \(x = 0, \tfrac{\pi}{3}, \pi\). Changing the domain for \(\theta\) first is what stops solutions being missed or wrongly included.
check: \(x + \tfrac{\pi}{6} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\), so \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{3}\). (\(\tfrac{5\pi}{2}\) is outside the shifted domain.)

fig.cap: 2cos(2x − π/3) = 1 on [0, π]: the curve meets y = 1 at x = 0, π/3 and π.

p: How many solutions does \(x^2 - 4x = k\) have? Think graphically: \(y = x^2 - 4x\) is a parabola with turning point \((2, -4)\), and \(y = k\) is a horizontal line. Two solutions if \(k > -4\), one if \(k = -4\), none if \(k < -4\).

The same thinking works for any family: \(e^x = k\) has one solution if \(k > 0\) and none otherwise; \(\sin x = k\) on \([0, 2\pi]\) has two solutions for \(-1 < k < 1\) except \(k = 0\), which has three (\(0, \pi, 2\pi\)), and one each for \(k = \pm 1\).
check: For what values of \(k\) does \(x^2 + k = 0\) have two solutions?

fig.cap: How many solutions does x² − 4x = k have? Count the meetings of the parabola with the line y = k: two for k > −4, one for k = −4, none for k < −4.

p: In the technology-active exam, a CAS solves most equations quickly, but marks are still lost. Always enter the domain restriction so that only valid solutions are returned. Give exact answers when the question asks for them. Check that the number of solutions makes sense by graphing. In extended answers, write the equation you solved before the result, so the method is visible.
Cancelling a factor that could be zero. Accepting solutions outside the domain of a log. Missing solutions when the domain is not \([0, 2\pi]\). Giving decimals when an exact answer is asked for.

topics.title: Algorithms and pseudocode
points: Pseudocode describes an algorithm in structured plain language: assignment (←), decisions (if … then … else … end if) and loops (for, while).
Trace an algorithm with a table that records each variable after every step.
Bisection: if \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, a root lies between; halve the interval and keep the half where the sign changes.
Newton’s method: \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\); it converges quickly near a root but can fail near a stationary point.
The trapezium rule is a loop that adds the areas of trapezia to approximate a definite integral.
topics.explain: Explain, as if to a friend, how the bisection method finds a root, and why it always works if the function is continuous and the starting values have opposite signs.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with solving equations, derivatives and definite integrals.

The big idea: many equations cannot be solved exactly, and many integrals cannot be found with an antiderivative. Numerical methods get as close as you like by repeating a simple step. The study design asks you to read, trace and write these methods as algorithms in pseudocode, a structured way of writing steps that is independent of any programming language.

Assignment uses an arrow: “x ← 3” stores 3 in x; “x ← x + 1” increases x by 1. Conditionals: “if … then … else … end if”. A for loop repeats a fixed number of times: “for i from 1 to 10 … end for”. A while loop repeats until a condition fails: “while … do … end while”. Functions are defined with “define f(x)” and give a result with “return”. Output uses “print”.
Indentation shows which lines belong inside a loop or condition. Read pseudocode one line at a time, as the computer would, and never skip ahead.

Trace this algorithm:
x ← 1
for i from 1 to 4
    x ← 2 × x + 1
end for
print x

Keep a table with a column for each variable. After i = 1, x = 3. After i = 2, x = 7. After i = 3, x = 15. After i = 4, x = 31. The output is 31. Tracing by hand like this is exactly what exam questions ask for, so practise writing the table neatly.
check: Trace: s ← 0; for k from 1 to 3: s ← s + k²; end for; print s. What is printed?
s becomes 1, then 5, then 14. The output is 14.

p: If a continuous function changes sign between \(a\) and \(b\), there is a root between them. Bisection repeatedly halves the interval. Compute the midpoint \(m\); if \(f(a)\) and \(f(m)\) have opposite signs, the root is in \([a, m]\); otherwise it is in \([m, b]\). Repeat until the interval is as small as required.

In pseudocode:
define f(x)
    return x³ − x − 1
a ← 1
b ← 2
while b − a > 0.001
    m ← (a + b) ÷ 2
    if f(a) × f(m) < 0 then
        b ← m
    else
        a ← m
    end if
end while
print (a + b) ÷ 2
check: Using bisection on \(f(x) = x^2 - 2\) starting with \([1, 2]\), what is the interval after one step?

fig.cap: Bisection on f(x) = x³ − x − 1: midpoints 1.5 (positive), then 1.25 (negative), then 1.375 (positive) close in on the root near 1.32.

p: Newton’s method uses the tangent line. From an estimate \(x_n\), follow the tangent to where it meets the \(x\)-axis: \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\).

Example: \(f(x) = x^3 - x - 1\), \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1\), \(x_0 = 1.5\). \(x_1 = 1.5 - \dfrac{0.875}{5.75} \approx 1.34783\); \(x_2 \approx 1.32520\); \(x_3 \approx 1.32472\). Three steps give five accurate decimal places, far faster than bisection.

It can fail. If \(f'(x_n)\) is close to zero (near a stationary point), the tangent is nearly flat and the next estimate is thrown far away; if \(f'(x_n) = 0\) the formula is undefined. A poor starting value can also lead to a different root.

In pseudocode:
define f(x)
    return x³ − x − 1
define df(x)
    return 3x² − 1
x ← 1.5
for i from 1 to 5
    x ← x − f(x) ÷ df(x)
end for
print x
check: Apply one step of Newton’s method to \(f(x) = x^2 - 2\) from \(x_0 = 1\).

fig.cap: One step of Newton’s method from x₀ = 1.5: follow the tangent down to the x-axis, landing at x₁ ≈ 1.348, much closer to the root.

notes.h: The trapezium rule as an algorithm
p: To approximate \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) with \(n\) strips of width \(h = \dfrac{b - a}{n}\), add the areas of the trapezia: each is \(\dfrac{h}{2}\big(f(x_{i}) + f(x_{i+1})\big)\).

In pseudocode:
h ← (b − a) ÷ n
total ← 0
for i from 0 to n − 1
    x ← a + i × h
    total ← total + (h ÷ 2) × (f(x) + f(x + h))
end for
print total

Updating a variable in the trace table before the line that changes it. Running a loop one time too many or too few. In bisection, keeping the wrong half. In Newton’s method, using f instead of f′ in the denominator, or forgetting that the method needs a non-zero derivative.

qs.q: In pseudocode, “t ← t × 2” means…
o: t is replaced by twice its current value

qs.q: For bisection on \([a, b]\), the method requires that…
Trace: x ← 10; while x > 1: x ← x ÷ 2; end while; print x. What is printed?
qs.a: x becomes 5, 2.5, 1.25, then 0.625, which stops the loop. The output is 0.625.

qs.q: When can Newton’s method fail?
qs.a: When the derivative at an estimate is zero or close to zero (near a stationary point), or when a poor starting value leads away from the wanted root.

qs.q: One Newton step for \(f(x) = x^2 - 5\) from \(x_0 = 2\) gives…
Trace: a ← 2; b ← 5; for i from 1 to 3: a ← a + b; b ← a − b; end for; print a, b.
s: Output: 16, 9. Each line uses the value just updated above it.

qs.q: Bisection on \(f(x) = x^2 - 3\) starts with \([1, 2]\). After one step the interval is…
Apply one step of Newton’s method to \(f(x) = x^3 - 2\) from \(x_0 = 1\).
n ← 1; while n < 20: n ← 2 × n; end while; print n. The output is…
qs.e: n takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32; the loop stops once n is no longer below 20.

qs.q: Use the trapezium rule with two strips to estimate \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 x^2\,dx\). Is it an over- or underestimate?
s: The exact value is \(\tfrac{8}{3}\). The curve is concave up, so the trapezia sit above it: an overestimate.

topics.title: Differentiation rules
points: Standard derivatives: \[\begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx}e^{kx} &= ke^{kx} & \frac{d}{dx}\log_e x &= \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{d}{dx}\sin(kx) &= k\cos(kx) & \frac{d}{dx}\cos(kx) &= -k\sin(kx) \\ \frac{d}{dx}\tan(kx) &= \frac{k}{\cos^2(kx)} \end{aligned}\]
Chain rule: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{du} \times \dfrac{du}{dx}\).
Product rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv) = u'v + uv'\). Quotient rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{u'v - uv'}{v^2}\).
Applications: tangents and normals, stationary points, maximum and minimum problems, rates of change.
Strictly increasing where \(f'(x) > 0\); strictly decreasing where \(f'(x) < 0\).
Linear approximation: \(f(x + h) \approx f(x) + h f'(x)\).
topics.explain: Explain when you would use the chain rule instead of the product rule.

qs.q: Differentiate \(\sin(3x)\).
Differentiate \(\log_e(x^2 + 1)\).
Differentiate \(xe^x\).
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}e^{3x} =\)
Differentiate \((x^2 + 1)^4\).
s: Chain rule: outside function \(u^4\), inside \(u = x^2 + 1\).

qs.q: Differentiate \(x^2e^x\).
s: Product rule with \(u = x^2\), \(v = e^x\): \(u' = 2x\), \(v' = e^x\).

qs.q: Differentiate \(\dfrac{\log_e x}{x}\).
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(2x) =\)
Find and classify the stationary point of \(y = x - \log_e x\), \(x > 0\).
s: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \dfrac{1}{x^2} > 0\), so it is a local minimum.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the Units 1 and 2 differentiation lesson and with exponential, logarithmic and circular functions.

The big idea: three rules, chain, product and quotient, extend differentiation from powers of \(x\) to every function in the course. With them, you can find the gradient of any curve and solve optimisation problems that were out of reach before.

A function inside another function needs the chain rule. Two functions multiplied need the product rule. One function divided by another needs the quotient rule. Simplify first where you can, since expanding or dividing through is often quicker than a rule.

Differentiate the outside function, leaving the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Examples: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(3x^2 + 1)^5 = 5(3x^2 + 1)^4 \cdot 6x = 30x(3x^2 + 1)^4\). \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\,e^{x^2} = 2x e^{x^2}\). \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e(4x - 1) = \dfrac{4}{4x - 1}\). \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\sin(3x) = 3\cos(3x)\).
Example (quotient): \(y = \dfrac{\sin x}{x}\). \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x\cos x - \sin x}{x^2}\). Factorise the answer when you need to solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\).

A function is not differentiable where its graph has a sharp corner, a break or a vertical tangent, or at the endpoints of a closed domain. To sketch \(f'\) from \(f\): stationary points of \(f\) become \(x\)-intercepts of \(f'\); where \(f\) increases, \(f'\) is above the axis; a point of inflection of \(f\) becomes a turning point of \(f'\).

The second derivative \(f''(x)\) measures how the gradient is changing. \(f'' > 0\) means concave up; \(f'' < 0\) means concave down; a point of inflection is where concavity changes. At a stationary point, \(f'' > 0\) indicates a local minimum and \(f'' < 0\) a local maximum.
A closed cylinder must hold 1000 cm³. Find the radius that minimises the surface area.

\(\pi r^2 h = 1000 \Rightarrow h = \dfrac{1000}{\pi r^2}\). \(A = 2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r h = 2\pi r^2 + \dfrac{2000}{r}\). \(\dfrac{dA}{dr} = 4\pi r - \dfrac{2000}{r^2} = 0 \Rightarrow r^3 = \dfrac{500}{\pi} \Rightarrow r \approx 5.42\) cm. \(\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2} = 4\pi + \dfrac{4000}{r^3} > 0\), so it is a minimum.
On a closed interval, compare the values of the function at the stationary points inside the interval and at both endpoints. The largest is the absolute maximum.
\(\dfrac{d}{dx}\tan(kx) = \dfrac{k}{\cos^2(kx)}\). Example: at \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{8}\), the derivative of \(\tan(2x)\) is \(\dfrac{2}{\cos^2\tfrac{\pi}{4}} = \dfrac{2}{\tfrac{1}{2}} = 4\).
For logarithms of a function, combine with the chain rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e\!\big(f(x)\big) = \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\). Example: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\log_e(x^2 + 1) = \dfrac{2x}{x^2 + 1}\).

Tangent: \(y - e = 2(x - e)\), so \(y = 2x - e\). The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, with gradient \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\): \(y - e = -\tfrac{1}{2}(x - e)\), so \(y = -\tfrac{1}{2}x + \tfrac{3e}{2}\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the differentiation rules and with anti-differentiation from Units 1 and 2.

The big idea: integration adds up small pieces. Its most visible use is area under a curve, but the same tool gives total change from a rate, average values and, in the probability lessons, probabilities for continuous variables. The fundamental theorem of calculus makes it calculable with antiderivatives.

\(\displaystyle\int (ax + b)^n dx = \frac{(ax + b)^{n+1}}{a(n + 1)} + c\) for \(n \ne -1\). \(\displaystyle\int \frac{1}{ax + b}\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\log_e(ax + b) + c\) for \(ax + b > 0\). \(\displaystyle\int \sin(kx)\,dx = -\frac{1}{k}\cos(kx) + c\). \(\displaystyle\int \cos(kx)\,dx = \frac{1}{k}\sin(kx) + c\). These reverse the chain rule only when the inside function is linear.
If you are asked to differentiate first and “hence” integrate, use the derivative to work backwards.
Example: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_e x) = \log_e x + 1\). So \(\displaystyle\int (\log_e x + 1)\,dx = x\log_e x + c\), and therefore \(\displaystyle\int \log_e x\,dx = x\log_e x - x + c\).

The fundamental theorem of calculus links area and antiderivatives: \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)\). The definite integral gives signed area: regions below the \(x\)-axis count as negative. Properties: \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f = -\int_b^a f\); \(\displaystyle\int_a^b f + \int_b^c f = \int_a^c f\); \(\displaystyle\int_a^b (kf + g) = k\int_a^b f + \int_a^b g\).
Find the area enclosed by \(y = x^2 - 4\) and the \(x\)-axis.

Intercepts at \(x = \pm 2\); the curve is below the axis between them. \(\displaystyle\int_{-2}^{2}(x^2 - 4)\,dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - 4x\right]_{-2}^{2} = -\frac{32}{3}\). Area \(= \tfrac{32}{3}\) square units.
Between two curves: \(y = x\) and \(y = x^2\) meet at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 1\), with the line on top. Area \(= \displaystyle\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{1}{3} = \tfrac{1}{6}\).

If you integrate a rate of change, you get the total change: \(\displaystyle\int_a^b v(t)\,dt\) is the change in position (displacement); the distance travelled is \(\displaystyle\int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt\). The average value of a function is the height of the rectangle with the same area over the interval.
The trapezium rule estimates an area with \(n\) strips of width \(h\): \(\dfrac{h}{2}\big(f(x_0) + 2f(x_1) + \dots + 2f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)\big)\). It overestimates when the curve is concave up.
Find the area enclosed between \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = \cos x\) for \(0 \le x \le \pi\). They meet where \(\tan x = 1\), at \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{4}\). Before that, cosine is on top; after it, sine is.

\(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/4} (\cos x - \sin x)\,dx = \big[\sin x + \cos x\big]_0^{\pi/4} = \sqrt{2} - 1\). \(\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi} (\sin x - \cos x)\,dx = \big[-\cos x - \sin x\big]_{\pi/4}^{\pi} = 1 + \sqrt{2}\). Total area \(= 2\sqrt{2}\). Integrating across the crossing without splitting would subtract one region from the other.
check: Why must an area integral be split where the curves cross?
The signed integral would subtract the region where the ‘top’ function is actually below, giving less than the true area.

A particle has velocity \(v = t^2 - 4t + 3\) m/s for \(0 \le t \le 3\). Velocity is zero at \(t = 1\) and \(t = 3\), and negative between them.

Displacement \(= \displaystyle\int_0^3 v\,dt = \left[\tfrac{t^3}{3} - 2t^2 + 3t\right]_0^3 = 0\): the particle ends where it started. Distance travelled \(= \displaystyle\int_0^1 v\,dt + \left|\int_1^3 v\,dt\right| = \tfrac{4}{3} + \tfrac{4}{3} = \tfrac{8}{3}\) m.

topics.title: Discrete random variables and the binomial distribution
points: A discrete probability distribution has \(0 \le \Pr(X = x) \le 1\) and \(\sum \Pr(X = x) = 1\).
\(\operatorname{E}(X) = \sum x\Pr(X = x)\). \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^2) - [\operatorname{E}(X)]^2\). \(\operatorname{sd}(X) = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\).
Binomial \(X \sim \operatorname{Bi}(n, p)\): \(n\) independent trials, each a success with probability \(p\). \[\Pr(X = x) = \binom{n}{x}p^x(1 - p)^{n - x}\]
Binomial mean \(\operatorname{E}(X) = np\); variance \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)\).
\(\operatorname{E}(aX + b) = a\operatorname{E}(X) + b\); \(\operatorname{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the Units 1 and 2 probability lesson, including combinations.

The big idea: a random variable turns the outcomes of an experiment into numbers, so that you can calculate averages and spreads. The binomial distribution is the model for counting successes in repeated independent trials, and it is the bridge to the sampling lesson at the end of the course.

A random variable assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. It is discrete if its values can be listed. Its probability distribution is a table, graph or rule giving \(\Pr(X = x)\) for each value. Two checks: every probability is between 0 and 1, and they add to 1.
\(X\) takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3.

\(\operatorname{E}(X) = 0(0.2) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.3) = 1.1\). \(\operatorname{E}(X^2) = 0 + 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7\). \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^2) - [\operatorname{E}(X)]^2 = 1.7 - 1.21 = 0.49\), so \(\operatorname{sd}(X) = 0.7\).

The mean is the long-run average, not the most likely value. If \(Y = 3X + 2\), then \(\operatorname{E}(Y) = 5.3\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y) = 9 \times 0.49 = 4.41\): adding a constant does not change the spread.

All four conditions must hold: a fixed number \(n\) of trials; each trial has two outcomes (success or failure); the probability of success \(p\) is the same in every trial; the trials are independent. Sampling without replacement from a small group fails the last two.
\(\Pr(X = x) = \dbinom{n}{x}p^x(1 - p)^{n - x}\). The coefficient counts the number of orders in which the successes can occur.
check: Is the number of aces in 5 cards dealt from one deck binomial?
No. The cards are dealt without replacement, so the probability changes from card to card and the trials are not independent.

fig.cap: The distribution of X ~ Bi(5, 0.2). It is positively skewed because p < 0.5; the mean np = 1.

p: A student guesses 5 multiple-choice questions, each with 4 options. \(X \sim \operatorname{Bi}(5, 0.25)\).

How many questions must be guessed so the probability of at least one correct is above 0.95? \(1 - 0.75^n > 0.95 \Rightarrow 0.75^n < 0.05 \Rightarrow n > \dfrac{\log_e 0.05}{\log_e 0.75} \approx 10.4\), so \(n = 11\). The inequality reverses because \(\log_e 0.75\) is negative.

The binomial distribution is symmetric when \(p = 0.5\), positively skewed when \(p < 0.5\) and negatively skewed when \(p > 0.5\); it becomes more symmetric as \(n\) grows. Conditional example: \(\Pr(X = 2 \mid X \ge 1) = \dfrac{\Pr(X = 2)}{\Pr(X \ge 1)}\).

notes.h: Building a distribution from an experiment
p: Toss two fair coins and let \(X\) be the number of heads. Outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT are equally likely, so \(\Pr(X = 0) = \tfrac{1}{4}\), \(\Pr(X = 1) = \tfrac{1}{2}\), \(\Pr(X = 2) = \tfrac{1}{4}\).

\(\operatorname{E}(X) = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{2}{4} = 1\). \(\operatorname{E}(X^2) = 0 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{4}{4} = 1.5\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = 1.5 - 1 = 0.5\). This matches the binomial formulas with \(n = 2\), \(p = 0.5\): \(np = 1\) and \(np(1 - p) = 0.5\).

p: \(\Pr(X = x) = kx\) for \(x = 1, 2, 3, 4\). The probabilities add to 1: \(k(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 10k = 1\), so \(k = 0.1\).

Write the distribution first, for example \(X \sim \operatorname{Bi}(10, 0.3)\), then the probability needed. Use the probability function for a single value, \(\Pr(X = 3)\), and the cumulative function for ranges, \(\Pr(X \le 2)\) or \(\Pr(2 \le X \le 5)\).
Translate words carefully: “at least 3” is \(\Pr(X \ge 3) = 1 - \Pr(X \le 2)\); “more than 3” is \(\Pr(X \ge 4)\); “at most 3” is \(\Pr(X \le 3)\); “fewer than 3” is \(\Pr(X \le 2)\).

points: A probability density function has \(f(x) \ge 0\) and \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx = 1\). \(\Pr(a < X < b) = \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\).
\(\operatorname{E}(X) = \displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x f(x)\,dx\). The median \(m\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{m} f(x)\,dx = 0.5\).
Normal distribution \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\): about 68% within \(\mu \pm \sigma\), 95% within \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\), 99.7% within \(\mu \pm 3\sigma\).
Standardise: \(Z = \dfrac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\), with \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\).
For a continuous variable, \(\Pr(X = a) = 0\).

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with definite integrals and with discrete random variables.

The big idea: when a variable can take any value in an interval, such as a time, a mass or a height, probabilities come from areas under a curve instead of from a table. The normal distribution is the most important continuous model, because so many measurements cluster symmetrically around an average.

A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, so probabilities are given by areas under a probability density function (pdf). The height of the pdf is not a probability and can be greater than 1. \(\Pr(a < X < b) = \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). The probability of any single exact value is zero, so \(<\) and \(\le\) give the same answer.
\(f(x) = kx(2 - x)\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\), and 0 elsewhere.
Total area 1: \(k\displaystyle\int_0^2 (2x - x^2)\,dx = k\left[x^2 - \tfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = \tfrac{4k}{3} = 1\), so \(k = \tfrac{3}{4}\).

\(\Pr(X < 1) = \tfrac{3}{4}\displaystyle\int_0^1 (2x - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{1}{2}\), as expected from symmetry. \(\operatorname{E}(X) = \displaystyle\int_0^2 x f(x)\,dx = 1\).

fig.cap: The pdf f(x) = 2x on [0, 1]. The median 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 splits the area into two halves.

p: The median \(m\) satisfies \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{m} f(x)\,dx = 0.5\). The \(p\)th percentile has area \(p\%\) to its left. \(\operatorname{Var}(X) = \operatorname{E}(X^2) - [\operatorname{E}(X)]^2\), where \(\operatorname{E}(X^2) = \displaystyle\int x^2 f(x)\,dx\).

A normal distribution is symmetric about its mean and described completely by \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). The mean, median and mode are equal. Changing \(\mu\) translates the curve; increasing \(\sigma\) makes it wider and lower, with the area still 1. The standard normal \(Z\) has mean 0 and standard deviation 1; a \(z\)-value is the number of standard deviations from the mean.

fig.cap: The standard normal curve. About 68% of the area lies within one standard deviation of the mean (shaded).

p: Heights are normal with \(\mu = 170\) cm and \(\sigma = 8\) cm.

\(\Pr(X > 186) = \Pr(Z > 2) \approx 0.025\), using the 95% rule: 5% lies outside two standard deviations, half of it above. For other values use technology and write the set-up, for example \(\Pr(160 < X < 175)\) with \(X \sim N(170, 8^2)\).
Inverse problem: the height exceeded by 10% of people. \(\Pr(Z < z) = 0.9\) gives \(z \approx 1.2816\), so \(x = 170 + 1.2816 \times 8 \approx 180.3\) cm.

notes.h: Worked example: median, mean and variance
p: \(f(x) = 2x\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\), and 0 elsewhere. Median: \(\displaystyle\int_0^m 2x\,dx = m^2 = 0.5\), so \(m = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.707\).

Mean: \(\operatorname{E}(X) = \displaystyle\int_0^1 2x^2\,dx = \tfrac{2}{3}\). \(\operatorname{E}(X^2) = \displaystyle\int_0^1 2x^3\,dx = \tfrac{1}{2}\). Variance: \(\tfrac{1}{2} - \tfrac{4}{9} = \tfrac{1}{18}\). The mean is below the median because the distribution has a longer tail to the left.

p: For the same pdf, \(\Pr(X > a) = 1 - a^2\). So \(\Pr(X > 0.5 \mid X > 0.25) = \dfrac{\Pr(X > 0.5)}{\Pr(X > 0.25)} = \dfrac{0.75}{0.9375} = 0.8\). The intersection of the two events is just \(X > 0.5\), because that event lies inside the other.

p: Before this lesson you should be confident with the binomial and normal distributions.

The big idea: we rarely know the true proportion of a population with some property, so we estimate it from a sample. Different samples give different estimates. This lesson describes how much they vary, and turns one sample into an interval that is likely to contain the true value.

A population proportion \(p\) is a fixed number, usually unknown. A sample proportion \(\hat{p} = \dfrac{\text{number in sample with the attribute}}{n}\) is calculated from one random sample and varies from sample to sample. The random variable \(\hat{P}\) describes that variation; its distribution is the sampling distribution.
For random samples, the number with the attribute is \(X \sim \operatorname{Bi}(n, p)\) and \(\hat{P} = \dfrac{X}{n}\), so exact probabilities for small samples come from the binomial distribution.
Suppose 30% of a large population has a certain attribute, so \(p = 0.3\), and a random sample of \(n = 10\) is taken.

\(\operatorname{E}(\hat{P}) = p\), so sample proportions centre on the true value. \(\operatorname{sd}(\hat{P}) = \sqrt{\dfrac{p(1 - p)}{n}}\), so larger samples vary less. To halve the standard deviation, the sample size must be multiplied by four. When \(n\) is large, \(\hat{P}\) is approximately normal with this mean and standard deviation.

An approximate 95% confidence interval for \(p\) is \(\hat{p} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}}\). The amount added and subtracted is the margin of error. For another confidence level replace 1.96 with the matching \(z\)-value: about 1.645 for 90% and 2.576 for 99%.
Example: 120 of 400 sampled voters support a proposal. \(\hat{p} = 0.3\). Margin of error \(= 1.96\sqrt{\dfrac{0.3 \times 0.7}{400}} = 0.045\). The interval is \((0.255, 0.345)\).

The population proportion is fixed; the interval is what varies. If many samples were taken and an interval calculated from each, about 95% of those intervals would contain \(p\). It is not correct to say there is a 95% probability that \(p\) lies in one particular calculated interval.
The sample proportion is always the midpoint of the interval, which lets you recover \(\hat{p}\) and \(n\) from a given interval.

Imagine taking thousands of random samples of the same size and recording \(\hat{p}\) for each. Plotted, the values form a roughly bell-shaped distribution centred on the true \(p\). Simulation on a calculator or computer shows this directly. As \(n\) increases, the distribution becomes narrower and more symmetric: larger samples give estimates that are more consistently close to \(p\).

It halves, because the sample size appears under a square root.

topics.title: Exam technique for Methods
points: Examination 1 is technology-free (short answers, exact values); Examination 2 is technology-active (multiple choice and extended response). Check the current specifications.
Give exact answers unless a decimal is asked for; follow the required number of decimal places.
Show the working that leads to each result, especially in “show that” and “hence” questions.
State domains, coordinates and units; label graphs fully.
Use technology for long calculations but write down what you solved.
topics.explain: Pick a past exam question you lost marks on. Write the full-mark solution and list the specific things the marking scheme rewarded.

p: Read this lesson once you have covered most of Units 3 and 4, and return to it before each practice exam.

The big idea: Methods exams reward precise communication as well as correct mathematics. Many students who understand the content lose marks to missing domains, unsimplified answers or invisible working. These habits are easy to fix with deliberate practice.

Examination 1 is completed without a calculator or notes. Questions are short and test core skills: algebra, exact values, differentiation and integration rules, and probability set-ups. Fluency matters, so practise by hand regularly through the year.

Examination 2 allows approved technology and a bound reference. It has a multiple-choice section and extended-response questions that build on one context across several parts. Formats, timing and the formula sheet can change, so check the current VCAA examination specifications and sample papers.

Unless a question asks for a decimal, give exact values: \(\log_e 3\), \(\tfrac{\pi}{6}\), \(2\sqrt{5}\), \(\tfrac{1}{e}\). Simplify fully. When a decimal is required, round only at the end, to the number of places asked for; rounding early can change the final digit and cost the mark.
Coordinates are written as \((x, y)\). Domains and ranges use correct notation. Answers to contextual questions need units and a sentence that answers the question asked.
check: A question asks for the exact solution of \(e^{x} = 5\). Is 1.609 acceptable?

p: In a “show that” question the answer is given, so every mark is for the working. Start from the given information and reach the result through clear, logical steps; do not start from the answer.

“Hence” means use the previous result. “Hence, or otherwise” allows another method, but the previous result is usually the quickest route. Even if you could not complete an earlier part, you may use its stated result in a later part.

Define functions once and reuse them, to avoid retyping errors. Restrict domains when solving. Use the graph to check the number and approximate values of solutions. For multiple-choice questions, technology can test each option, but be wary of time.
Write the mathematics you entered. “\(\Pr(X > 120)\) where \(X \sim N(100, 15^2)\) is 0.0912” earns method marks that “0.0912” alone does not.

p: Functions: missing the domain of an inverse; composite functions that are not defined. Calculus: forgetting the chain rule; not splitting area at an intercept; leaving out \(+c\) where needed. Probability: “at least” and “more than” confused; variance and standard deviation confused; conditional probability with the wrong denominator. Equations: solutions outside the domain; missing solutions of circular equations.

Through the year, use Review on this site daily and do mixed quizzes across topics. In the last months, do complete past papers under timed conditions, then mark them using the examination reports, which explain what earned marks. Keep a list of every mark lost and why. Repeat questions you got wrong a week later.

Spending too long on one hard part. Giving decimals when exact values are required. Not reading the final sentence of a question, which often specifies the form of the answer. Leaving multiple-choice questions blank.
